zones.name: Application Core
zones.description: Central app coordination hub bridging GoToBedCore logic with app-layer services, state management, and UI wiring.
insights: 10 entry points — wide API surface, consider consolidating exports

10+ entry points across config, models, services, and UI indicate this zone conflates orchestration with component implementation; consolidate initialization logic into AppEnvironment and separate pure-logic imports (Schedule, Validation, ScheduleCalculator, Persistence) into a dedicated app-logic zone

MenuViewModel and SettingsWindowController are service implementations that should establish clear ownership (who instantiates them, who retains them, who triggers updates) to avoid scattered state mutation

Bidirectional coupling with view-layer (4 imports each direction) and scheduling-engine (8 imports in, 6 out) indicates this zone is the integration hub; document the initialization sequence and state-flow contracts explicitly
Zone "application-core" has files across 8 directories — consider consolidating under a dedicated directory

AppEnvironment is the sole site that mediates the scheduler→overlay boundary via a closure injected at SchedulerEngine init; this runtime inversion prevents the bidirectional scheduling-engine ↔ application-core coupling from becoming a circular import — it is currently undocumented and invisible to static analysis

Schedule.swift contains a silent backward-compatibility Decodable migration (missing submessage and dismissChallenge keys are silently defaulted) with no migration version or deprecation notice — callers cannot distinguish migrated from canonical data

MenuContent.swift carries a redundant `import GoToBedCore` — no GoToBedCore symbol is directly referenced in the file; the file's own comment states it has no direct domain dependency, but the import list contradicts that claim and creates a false coupling signal for static analysis tools

The closure-injection boundary in AppEnvironment.init (onFire: (Schedule) -> Void) that breaks the scheduler→overlay cycle is currently undocumented; losing this comment or refactoring SchedulerEngine.init naively would silently reintroduce the circular import it prevents

zones.name: Overlay Interaction System

insights: High coupling (0.75) — 4 imports target "application-core"

Low cohesion (0.25) conflates state management (DismissChallengeState), window control (OverlayWindow), and UI presentation (WeekdayPicker); move WeekdayPicker to view-layer where other UI components live, keep DismissChallengeState and OverlayWindow focused on orchestration
4 imports to application-core indicate state is pulled directly from services; use @Environment or pass state via view parameters to decouple window management from core services

OverlayWindow's relationship to OverlayController (in scheduling-engine) is critical but implicit; document window lifecycle (creation, presentation trigger, dismissal flow) so future changes don't break initialization order

DismissChallengeState already accepts an injectable RandomNumberGenerator in its designated init for deterministic test control — this is the only GoToBedKit service that applies this pattern; it demonstrates the approach is feasible and could be replicated in SchedulerEngine for timer/notification injection

zones.name: Scheduling Engine
zones.description: Core scheduling execution and overlay orchestration for bedtime prompt lifecycle.
insights: High coupling (0.79) — 6 imports target "application-core"

Very low cohesion (0.21) with Log utility mixed alongside service implementations—extract Log to application-core or a foundation layer; logging is a cross-cutting concern that should not require coupling to the scheduler

High coupling (0.79) with 8 imports from application-core identifies this as a critical junction; SchedulerEngine bridges core scheduling logic to OverlayController, which bridges to UI—document this flow and ensure each component's responsibility is explicit

OverlayController's 1-import dependency on dismisschallengestate-overlaywindow plus heavy reliance on external services suggests complex initialization—add integration tests validating the scheduler→overlay→window activation sequence to prevent lifecycle bugs

SchedulerEngine imports AppKit solely to observe NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification and NSSystemClockDidChangeNotification; this hides an AppKit process requirement inside a service that is otherwise pure Foundation/Combine logic, preventing the engine from running in a non-AppKit test host without a real NSWorkspace

SchedulerEngine's AppKit dependency is not declared in its public interface — callers treating it as a Foundation-only scheduling service will discover the implicit NSApplication requirement only at link or runtime, not at the import boundary

SchedulerEngine.stop() removes every observer from both NSWorkspace.shared.notificationCenter and NotificationCenter.default in a single loop (line 82), but start() registers didWakeNotification exclusively to the workspace center and clock/timezone notifications exclusively to NotificationCenter.default — the double-removal is accidentally harmless (both centers silently ignore unregistered observers) but diverges from the add pattern, making it easy for a future observer added to a third center to be silently not removed

Log.swift in GoToBedCore declares Log.scheduler, Log.overlay, and Log.lifecycle as public API — three categories that name GoToBedKit operational subsystems, not GoToBedCore domain concerns; only Log.persistence is a genuine Core concern; the others embed Kit-deployment vocabulary into Core's exported surface, preventing Core from being used independently without advertising scheduler and overlay namespaces

OverlayController.teardown(animated:) captures previousActivationPolicy by value in its completion closure at line 80; if dismiss() starts the 0.2 s animation and present() is called before it completes, the completion handler fires and calls setActivationPolicy(.accessory) while the new overlay is already showing — at that point the app reverts from .regular to .accessory policy, potentially losing the key-focus state the comment at line 38 says is required for the borderless window to receive Esc

OverlayController animated teardown races with re-presentation: dismiss() starts a 0.2 s animation and captures previousActivationPolicy by value in the completion closure (line 80). If present() is called before the animation completes, the completion handler still fires and resets activation policy to .accessory while the new overlay window expects .regular for key focus. This can make Esc unreachable on the replacement overlay without any error signal.

SchedulerEngine.stop() calls both ws.removeObserver(o) and dnc.removeObserver(o) for every entry in observers (line 82), but the observers were registered to different centers in start(): didWakeNotification to NSWorkspace.shared.notificationCenter and clock/timezone notifications to NotificationCenter.default. The mismatched removal is a silent no-op today but diverges from the registration pattern; a future observer added to a third center would leak without any compiler or runtime warning.

Log.swift in GoToBedCore declares Log.scheduler, Log.overlay, and Log.lifecycle — categories naming GoToBedKit runtime subsystems — as public API on the Core package. Only Log.persistence reflects a Core-layer concern. The Kit-operational categories couple Core's public interface to Kit's deployment structure, preventing Core from being distributed or tested independently without carrying scheduler and overlay namespace declarations.

zones.name: UI View Layer
zones.description: SwiftUI presentation layer assembling settings, menu bar, overlay, and compatibility shims.
insights: Low cohesion (0.19) — files are loosely related, consider splitting this zone
High coupling (0.81) — 11 imports target "application-core"

Low cohesion (0.19) mixing four distinct UI surfaces without internal relationships—organize MenuContent, OverlayView, SettingsView into feature subdirectories (menu-bar/, settings-ui/, overlay-ui/) to improve structure and discoverability

Compat.swift bundled with UI components indicates platform compatibility logic is scattered; extract platform-specific adapters to a separate layer so compatibility concerns don't bleed into feature views

11 imports to application-core show this zone computes UI state directly from business logic; profile whether views are rendering pre-computed state or pulling raw models—push aggregation upstream to reduce view complexity

SettingsView injects both Store (reactive read path via @EnvironmentObject) and AppEnvironment (write path and actions) simultaneously; this dual-injection exposes the full persistence stack directly to view code rather than flowing reads through AppEnvironment's coordinator, breaking the single-owner intent for Store

SettingsView accesses store.schedules directly via @EnvironmentObject var store: Store, bypassing AppEnvironment's coordinator role for the read path; this creates a second, uncoordinated entry point to the persistence layer from the view layer and undermines the Store-as-single-source invariant

OverlayView.clockText(_:) allocates a new DateFormatter on every invocation (lines 101-104); because it is called by a TimelineView updating every second for the life of the overlay, this causes one expensive ICU locale-loading allocation per second that a static cached formatter would eliminate entirely

OverlayView.clockText(_:) constructs a fresh DateFormatter inside the function body on every call (lines 101-104). TimelineView fires it every second. DateFormatter initialization loads ICU calendar and locale data and is one of the most expensive object-creation operations in Foundation. Promoting the formatter to a private static let field would eliminate all per-tick allocation with no behavioral change.

The 4 circular dependency chains reported by static analysis are prevented from manifesting as circular imports at runtime exclusively by AppEnvironment's closure injection pattern — the actual Swift module import graph is acyclic, but the runtime call graph is not; this distinction exists nowhere in the codebase documentation and is a single-point-of-knowledge risk

GoToBedApp.swift is the only file that imports both GoToBedCore and GoToBedKit simultaneously, correctly placing cross-tier wiring at the executable composition root; the import itself is not a layering violation but means any GoToBedCore type added to GoToBedApp.swift carries no import cost signal that would alert reviewers to a potential layering drift

The Schedule struct in GoToBedCore functions as an implicit cross-target DTO spanning all three targets (Core, Kit, executable), bundling domain logic (validation, Decodable migration), scheduling parameters, and presentation data (message text, appearance) in a single type — all five zones import it, so any field addition or serialization change has monorepo-wide impact with no interface boundary to absorb it

The bidirectional application-core ↔ scheduling-engine coupling is load-bearing: AppEnvironment reads eight types from GoToBedCore through SchedulerEngine's gateway and injects the result back into OverlayController; extracting this wiring into an explicit scheduler-to-overlay protocol (e.g., OverlayTriggering) would make the data flow visible as a named interface rather than an anonymous closure

Sources/GoToBed/UI/ contains files from four distinct zones (appearance-settings, application-core, overlay-interaction, view-layer) with no subdirectory separation; the flat directory makes it impossible to determine a file's zone membership from its path alone, increasing the risk of zone boundary violations going unnoticed during review

OverlayController's activation-policy restoration is not cancellable once an animated teardown starts: the completion closure holds the only reference to the captured policy value and there is no mechanism to abort or supersede it if present() is called mid-animation. A generation counter or weak cancellation token on each teardown call would allow subsequent presents to invalidate stale completion handlers without requiring synchronous (non-animated) teardown paths.
